analysis.one_liner: Demotes high-cost lenders to last place in consumer bankruptcy and eases the means test for their victims.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by two Democratic senators in July 2008, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a lender charges an annual percentage rate above roughly 36% (including fees), this bill would have pushed that lender's claim to the back of the line in a consumer bankruptcy, behind everyone else the debtor owes, and would have transferred any liens securing that debt to the bankruptcy estate. It also would have exempted people driven into bankruptcy by such loans from the mandatory 'means test' that can force them out of Chapter 7 and into a repayment plan. In practice, a family drowning in payday or other high-rate debt would have had a better chance of a fresh start, and the high-cost lender would have recovered little or nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose bankruptcies were triggered by very high-rate credit. Their other creditors would be paid first, high-cost lenders' claims would be subordinated to all other claims, and any lien securing the high-cost debt would go to the bankruptcy estate rather than staying with the lender [S2][S3]. Debtors pushed into bankruptcy by high-cost loans would also be shielded from dismissal or forced conversion under the 'substantial abuse' means test [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers bankrupted by very high-rate loans

how_it_helps.text: Any claim arising from a 'high cost consumer credit transaction' — a consumer loan with an APR above the lesser of 15% plus the 30-year Treasury yield or 36%, counting fees — would be subordinated to all other claims in bankruptcy, meaning the high-cost lender gets paid only after every other creditor [S2][S3].
Any lien securing such a subordinated claim would be transferred to the bankruptcy estate, stripping the lender of collateral [S2][S3].

A debtor whose petition resulted from a high-cost loan would be excluded from the mandatory means-test dismissal or conversion to Chapter 11 or 13, so they could not be pushed out of Chapter 7 because of that debt [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost consumer lenders — such as payday and other subprime lenders whose rates and fees clear the roughly 36% threshold — would recover far less, or nothing, when a borrower files for bankruptcy, and would lose collateral liens. Some of that cost could be passed on to other borrowers through higher prices or tighter lending [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: High-cost lenders and their industry allies would argue that making their claims nearly worthless in bankruptcy raises the risk of lending to financially fragile borrowers, so lenders would either charge even more or stop serving them, shrinking credit access for the people the bill is meant to help [S2].

Because the APR definition counts costs and fees, the roughly 36% cutoff could sweep in some lenders well below the stereotype of a payday shop, and liens transferred to the estate would add complexity and disputes to bankruptcy cases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers at the mercy of very high-rate credit, the bill offered a meaningful shift: their other obligations would come first, the lender's collateral would be lost, and the means test could not be used against them because of that debt. The honest trade-off is that lenders facing near-total loss in bankruptcy would likely raise prices or reduce credit to risky borrowers, so the protection for people in bankruptcy could come at the cost of costlier or scarcer credit for people not yet in bankruptcy. The design is targeted — the threshold tracks Treasury yields and caps at 36% — but it does not address the underlying high-rate lending itself, only its consequences in court.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, joined by Sen. Richard Durbin, introduced the bill on July 14, 2008 [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the bill's only action [S5].
The Judiciary Committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost consumer lenders are better off, because they keep full priority for their claims and keep their collateral liens in consumer bankruptcies. Bankrupt consumers gained nothing; they remain subject to the means test and to repayment demands from high-rate lenders [S5][S2].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders, who keep full bankruptcy priority

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Consumer Credit Fairness Act on July 14, 2008 [S1][S3].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; the bill's only referral destination
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on July 14, 2008 — no markup, no vote, no report to the floor [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape never got tested; the bill's only support on record was two Democratic senators, and no recorded opponent ever acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: High-cost consumer lenders (payday, title, and other subprime lenders)
industries.note: The bill would have subordinated their claims to all other creditors and stripped their liens when a borrower they lent to at above roughly 36% APR files for bankruptcy, leaving them with little or nothing. Their interest in the bill ran directly against bankrupt consumers, who would have paid other debts first [S2][S3].

Issuers whose penalty rates and fees push a cardholder's effective APR past the threshold would have faced the same subordination and lien transfer; issuers staying under the cutoff would be unaffected and, as senior creditors, would actually be paid ahead of subordinated high-cost claims [S3].
